projects.title: Drew Breunig's scientific-method skill: stop the agent's silent edits
projects.what: An experience report on agents (Claude, but also GPT and GLM) that silently changed many parameters during ML experiments, and the skill Drew wrote to fix it. In short: a procedure sheet that makes the agent work like a rigorous scientist instead of an over-eager intern.
projects.how: A skill is an instruction file the agent loads when the task calls for it. This one enforces 3 rules: ground hypotheses in observations, run experiments to prove or disprove them, freeze variables and change one thing at a time. The cost: each experiment setup must be approved by hand. He notes autoresearch harnesses (the tooling around a model for autonomous research) avoid the issue because their prompts already carry this kind of methodology.
projects.who: Current models are proactive: an offhand remark becomes a reason to change five things. Fine for simple web work, but for costly work (ML experiments, an ops pipeline, a financial model) you need a heavy hand. Reusable tip: for delicate tasks, give the agent an explicit procedure (one change at a time, log every step in a journal.md).
projects.try: Free article. The skill itself is not published in the tweets. Site not reachable during this run, details limited to the thread.

projects.title: SlopCodeBench: what happens when you tell the agent "you own this code"
projects.what: Dex Horthy tests on SlopCodeBench (an eval by @GOrlanski and team that measures code quality over time) a tip from the official Fable 5.2 prompting guide: telling the model "you own this codebase and will be working in it over time".
projects.how: He compares two prompts on the same challenges: "just solve" (build the feature) vs "you own it". Early results: less duplicated code and more tests with "you own it". On one challenge, 8/8 passes vs 4/8. The stock prompt produced 3 duplicate implementations of the same function, while "you own it" created a reusable interface and deleted a large module in favor of a better abstraction. But token cost and duration were higher at every checkpoint, and in one case early tests locked in bad behavior.
projects.who: When you vibe code an internal tool that will live for months, the real danger is slop: code that works but piles up duplicates. One line of context in your CLAUDE.md can change how the agent behaves.
projects.try: Preliminary results (still early in the campaign). License and benchmark link not given in the tweets.

projects.title: Amp "Puck in the car": talk to your coding agent while driving
projects.what: A car mode for Puck, the voice assistant of Amp (Sourcegraph's coding agent). In short, a voice ChatGPT, but plugged into your projects and agent threads.
projects.how: You talk, it listens and answers out loud, using STT (speech-to-text: your voice becomes text) and TTS (text-to-speech: its answer becomes voice). A user (@ClaytonFarr) praises two choices: it does not make the little "mmm, ok" sounds that break your train of thought, and it knows when to start and stop talking. Puck works above Amp's other threads, spaces and projects: a steering layer, not one more agent.
projects.who: Follow up on or restart your agents without a screen, while commuting. @sqs adds that the call button can now be set as a global OS shortcut.
projects.try: Available in Amp. Price not given in the tweets. Site not reachable during this run, details limited.

projects.title: The Scout: a $25 Wi-Fi camera that gives your agent eyes
projects.what: A magnetic camera for the fridge, pantry, door or pets that your agent can check.
projects.how: You order it by telling your agent to read a page and help you buy one. Relayed by @dexhorthy ("heard very cool things").
